Neonatal Tiger snakes emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of 17 cm [Lb = 17 cm] and a body mass of 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams]. These newborns are immediately independent, relying on endogenous yolk reserves for a brief period before commencing active foraging on small lizards and frogs. Hatchlings are remarkably well-developed, displaying the characteristic banded pattern that gives the species its common name. Their small size at birth, however, places them at considerable risk from avian and mammalian predators, and mortality during the first year of life is correspondingly high. The relatively modest investment per offspring, reflected in the 4.5 gram [Wwb = 4.5 gram] birth weight, is offset by large clutch sizes and a reproductive strategy centered on high fecundity rather than intensive parental care. In the temperate wetlands and coastal habitats they occupy across southern Australia, these neonatal snakes must quickly learn to hunt effectively to fuel their rapid growth. The combination of a small starting size and an environment with pronounced seasonal fluctuations in prey availability shapes the early life history of this species in profound ways.

Female Tiger snakes attain reproductive maturity at a snout-vent length of 65 cm [Lp = 65 cm], a size that is typically reached between two and three years of age under favorable conditions. This threshold marks the onset of gonadal activation and the ability to produce viable offspring. Females generally delay their first reproductive event until they have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support gestation, a process that is energetically demanding in this viviparous species. Gravid individuals become noticeably heavier and more robust as they approach parturition. The pubertal size of 65 cm [Lp = 65 cm] reflects a compromise between the advantages of early reproduction and the need to allocate resources toward continued somatic growth. Females that breed too early may compromise their own survival or the quality of their offspring. In the field, researchers identify pubertal females by palpation of developing follicles and by monitoring the smallest females observed in copulation. The onset of breeding is also influenced by local thermal conditions and the abundance of prey such as the introduced cane toad, which varies considerably across the species' range.

Under controlled captive conditions maintained at a constant 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the maximum longevity of the Tiger snake has been recorded at approximately 14.1 years [am = approximately 14.1 years]. This figure, derived from a long-term captive colony, likely exceeds the typical lifespan achieved in the wild, where predation, disease, and environmental stressors impose additional mortality. Nevertheless, the 14.1 year [am = 14.1 year] maximum lifespan places Notechis scutatus among the longer-lived elapids, a pattern that may be linked to its relatively large body size and the energetic constraints of its cool-temperate habitat. at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] At the same thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], reproductive data collected from captive females reveal that individuals produce between 20 and 30 young per clutch [N_R_i = between 20 and 30 young per clutch], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This annual breeding cycle aligns with the seasonal availability of prey and the need for females to regain body condition between reproductive events.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in this species, with males ultimately reaching a snout-vent length of 120 cm [Li = 120 cm] and a maximum body mass of 2200 grams [Wwi = 2200 grams], while females attain a smaller ultimate size of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] in snout-vent length and 1400 grams [Wwi = 1400 grams] in body mass. This pattern is typical of many elapid snakes, where larger male body size is advantageous in male-male combat for access to receptive females. The 1400 gram [Wwi = 1400 gram] adult female mass represents a more than 300-fold increase over the 4.5 gram birth weight, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory this species undergoes. Males, achieving 2200 grams [Wwi = 2200 grams], are among the largest individuals in their genus. The discrepancy in ultimate size between the sexes is also reflected in their foraging ecology, as larger males can subdue larger prey items. Females, in contrast, allocate a greater proportion of their energy budget to reproduction. The 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] and 120 cm [Li = 120 cm] snout-vent length maxima for females and males, respectively, have been documented in multiple populations across the species' range, with some regional variation attributed to local prey availability and thermal regimes.

The reproductive output of female Tiger snakes, measured under the controlled thermal conditions of a captive colony at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], equates to approximately 20 to 30 live young per year [Ri = approximately 20 to 30 live young per year] when combined with a single annual clutch [F_R_i = single annual clutch]. At a body size of 136.7 cm snout-vent length, which represents a large adult female, the per capita daily reproductive rate is meaningfully expressed through this combination of clutch size and frequency. The 20 to 30 offspring per clutch [N_R_i = 20 to 30 offspring per clutch] born in a single parturition event are fully developed and measure approximately 17 cm [Lb = approximately 17 cm] at birth, immediately capable of subduing small vertebrate prey. This high fecundity is an adaptation to the high mortality rates experienced by juvenile snakes, ensuring that at least a few individuals from each cohort survive to reproductive age. The annual reproductive cycle, timed to coincide with the austral spring and summer, allows females to give birth when prey is most abundant and ambient temperatures are favorable for neonatal activity. This reproductive strategy, combining large litters with a single annual breeding event, is characteristic of many temperate-zone elapids.
